KEY MESSAGE 1...Cool and dry through Wednesday

Broad high pressure continues building eastward from the 
midwest/Great Lakes through tonight and tomorrow, then is slated to 
track off more to the north and east into the Canadian Maritimes 
closer to Thursday morning. Guidance has this high pressure 
strengthening to around 1040 mb, which will allow for upper level 
temperatures to drop and for continued dry conditions across 
southern New England. Strong high pressure will also support clear 
skies and slackening winds heading into tonight; light to calm winds 
and clear skies will allow for strong radiational cooling to take 
hold tonight. Lows in parts of the interior may fall into the teens. 
Elsewhere, expect lows to fall into the 20s with temperatures 
remaining just at or below freezing along the immediate coast. 
Dewpoints this afternoon already fell to as low as the lower teens, 
which is a trend that is expected to continue through Wednesday. 925 
mb temperatures remain below 0C into part of Wednesday night before 
the approaching coastal storm brings warmer air aloft back into the 
region. Some higher level clouds will start to build in as well 
heading into Thursday morning, which will limit the extent of 
radiational cooling for Wednesday night. These clouds look to build 
in from south to north, so temperatures towards the southern 
coastlines will likely not be as low as tonight's (though it will 
still be cold).

KEY MESSAGE 2...A coastal storm impacts the region Thanksgiving 
afternoon and night, possibly lingering into Friday morning, with 
dangerous marine conditions, coastal flooding and beach erosion, 
strong winds, and periods of heavy rainfall. Details regarding each 
hazard are below. 

Timing: 12z models continue a slower trend for the onset of the rain 
Thu, due to the large amplitude ridge over New England and its 
associated dry air. Therefore, much of Thu morning is trending dry, 
with rain overspreading the region south to north in the afternoon, 
then heavy at times late day, evening and overnight. This will 
impact travel, especially at night.

Rain: given progressive system with dry slot rapidly overspreading 
the region late Thu night/early Fri morning, yielding a relatively 
short duration rain event. While there will be periods of heavy rain 
late Thu into Thu night in response to 60-70 kt low level easterly 
jet, shorter duration event should limit rainfall to 1-2 inches. 
This combined with lots of capacity currently in rivers and streams, 
not expecting any freshwater flooding, other than nuisance/minor 
street-highway flooding at times. It will become a chilly windswept 
rain during the afternoon and evening, with temps in the 40s away 
from the south coast (cool temps aloft combined with wet bulbing and 
CAD signature with coastal low and high to the NE). Moderating Thu 
night as winds shift to the SE and eventually SW late. 

Coastal Flooding: high astronomical/king tides will combine with 
strong onshore flow later Thu, Thu night into early Fri for 
potential coastal flooding and beach erosion. Coastal low moving 
north up the coast from the Mid Atlantic, will combine with a strong 
1040 mb high over the Maritimes Thu for a period of strong easterly 
onshore winds of 20-30 mph, gusting to 45 to 55 mph. Given the 
progressive nature/fast moving coastal low, storm surge will be 
limited to 1-1.5 ft. However, given the high astronomical tides, 
this may be sufficient for coastal flooding and sufficient wave 
action for erosion. As with all coastal flood events, timing will be 
critical. As of now, it appears the strongest wind and greatest 
storm surge will coincide with the lower of the two tides, the Thu 
night tide cycle. The Thu afternoon and Fri morning to midday tides 
are much higher. Given the reasons above, we should be spared a 
significant event. If the system slows down a bit more and the 
strongest winds and largest surge occur closer to the Fri 
morning/early afternoon high tide, then a low probability of 
moderate coastal flooding and beach erosion event is possible. 
However, given the progressive nature of the system, that appears 
unlikely at the moment, but requires monitoring later model trends.  

Wind: Coastal low moving up the coast combining with a 1040 mb high 
over New England early Thu, along with 60-70kt low level ESE jet 
will yield a period of strong winds late Thu into Thu night. GFS and 
RRFS are the strongest of the guid, with 75-80kt low level jet. Much 
of the guidance has this low level jet maxing out over the Mid Atlc 
into PA/NJ/NYC/LI late Thu, then slowly weakening as it moves 
northeast over SNE and into Northern New England, as it ejects into 
the large amplitude ridge. Model soundings support wind gusts up to 
45 kt/50 mph along the coasts. Given this support along with the 
synoptic setting, we will hoist wind advisories for this region. 
It's possible later shifts may need to expand the wind advisory to 
the high terrain
